name: Spencer Seedless

origin.raised_by: Propagated and promoted by John F. Spencer

history: An apetalous, largely seedless apple propagated by John F. Spencer of Grand Junction, Colorado, after about a decade of trials, and promoted around 1905 as a future commercial apple. Another account traces the tree to Virginia via Wisconsin in the 1850s. It reached the UK National Fruit Trials from Long Ashton in 1970.

look.description: Large to very large, flattish pale-green apple with a mottled red flush when fully ripe; the core is tiny and usually seedless.

taste.summary: Dense, crisp and rather dry flesh that is mildly sweet, low in acid and without aroma. One enthusiast finds it pleasant; the National Fruit Collection rates the flavour very poor. Its interest is botanical rather than culinary.

tree.notes: The flowers have no petals and no stamens, so the tree barely seems to blossom; fruit sets without pollination (parthenocarpy), and any seeds come from stray cross-pollination. Described as hardy and prolific.

pollination.notes: Sets fruit without pollination, but its petal-less flowers give almost no pollen, so it is useless as a pollinator. Very late: Brogdale records full bloom around 23 May.

climate.best_climates: Recorded from the irrigated fruit district of western Colorado and grown in English collections; described as cold-hardy.

health.other: No disease information found. Early promoters hoped the seedless fruit would starve codling moth larvae.

grow_notes: A curiosity for collectors: it crops without a pollinator and keeps a long time, but eating quality is modest. The late flowering helps it avoid spring frosts.

name: Splendour

origin.parentage: Unknown; suspected Red Dougherty x Golden Delicious, not confirmed by genetic analysis

history: Discovered in 1948 by Charles Roberts at Napier and introduced commercially in the 1960s; long a popular New Zealand dessert apple. It is an ancestor of Pacific Rose (Sciros) and Aurora Golden Gala.

look.description: Medium-large, ribbed, conical apple with thin pale greenish-yellow skin, a soft pink to orange streaked blush and green lenticels.

taste.summary: Crisp, firm and juicy yellowish-white flesh with a sweet, low-acid flavour, a little richer than Golden Delicious and firmer in texture. Pleasant rather than aromatic.

tree.notes: Reliable, heavy cropper that bears on both spurs and tips. The fruit hangs well on the tree but has thin skin and bruises easily.

pollination.notes: Group 4 (Orange Pippin; Brogdale full bloom around 15 May).

climate.best_climates: Warm temperate climates like Hawke's Bay and California; one US nursery lists it as low-chill for zones 5-10.
climate.poor_climates: Cool short seasons may not ripen it well because it is late; handling damage limits it as a market apple.

health.other: One US nursery rates its disease resistance excellent and its fire-blight resistance among the best; bruises easily.

grow_notes: Plant in a warm, sunny site and handle the fruit gently at picking. Partly a tip-bearer, so avoid hard spur pruning.

name: American Summer Pearmain
history: An old American summer apple of unrecorded origin, first described in 1817 and long valued in eastern US home orchards. It is a parent of Meku.

look.description: Medium, oblong-conical yellow-green apple flushed and streaked with red to purplish red.

taste.summary: Very tender, almost melting, juicy yellow flesh with a sweet, mildly subacid and pleasantly aromatic flavour. Picked early it is crisper and sweeter; left longer it softens and becomes better for pies.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-Sep, straight from the tree; keeps about a week

tree.notes: Smallish upright tree, easy for beginners. Fruit ripens over a period, so pick in several passes.

pollination.notes: Group 2 (Orange Pippin; Brogdale full bloom around 5-6 May).

climate.best_climates: Orange Pippin lists it as cold-hardy and suited to cool, warm and cold summers in temperate regions.
climate.poor_climates: No specific reports; very hot summers ripen it early and soften it.

health.other: Average general disease resistance, with some susceptibility to powdery mildew and fire blight.

grow_notes: A good early dessert apple for small gardens; plant with an early-flowering partner. Eat or cook promptly, as the fruit does not keep.

name: Sweet Bough
history: An early American sweet apple described by 1817 and widely grown in eastern North America under many names; also once wrongly sold as 'Washington'.

look.description: Large, conical to oblong pale greenish-yellow apple, occasionally with a faint blush.

taste.summary: Very tender, juicy white flesh with a honeyed, almost acid-free sweetness and only slight aroma. Admirers value it as an early sweet apple; critics find it one-dimensional and soon mealy.

tree.notes: Small tree and heavy bearer with large, strongly scented blossom; responds well to thinning.

pollination.notes: Listed by a US nursery as mid-season flowering (taken here as group 3); needs a partner.

climate.best_climates: Eastern North American summers; a US nursery lists it for zones 5-9.

health.other: Described as disease-hardy; a low-spray grower in Massachusetts reports it largely disease-free.

grow_notes: A compact, productive tree for an early sweet apple; thin the fruitlets for size and eat within a couple of weeks of picking.

name: Sweet Delicious

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York
origin.raised_by: Richard Wellington, New York State Agricultural Experiment Station

history: Raised in 1911 by Richard Wellington at Geneva from Deacon Jones crossed with Delicious; a sister of Orleans from the same cross.

look.description: Large, ribbed, truncate-conical greenish-yellow apple flushed reddish orange with red streaks and many russet dots.

taste.summary: Firm, fine, creamy-white flesh that becomes melting; very sweet with an aromatic flavour and little acidity.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records full bloom around 15 May, which corresponds to group 4.

climate.best_climates: Inferred from its New York breeding: temperate climates with warm summers.

grow_notes: A very sweet keeping apple for collectors; grow like Delicious in a sunny, open site with a mid-season pollinator.

name: Tumanga

origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Schoener aus Nordhausen

history: Bred at Muencheberg in the 1930s (German Wikipedia gives 1935, Orange Pippin 1930) from Cox's Orange Pippin and Schoener aus Nordhausen, and marketed in East Germany from 1960 as Tumanga; in the West and at Brogdale it is known as Auralia. It is a parent of Pikkolo.

look.description: Small-to-medium, flat apple with smooth yellowish-green skin and a mottled orange-red cheek.

taste.summary: Juicy, tender, fine-grained yellowish-white flesh with a delicate sweet-sharp balance and a pleasant aromatic, perfumed character from its Cox parent. The flavour builds in store and is best from mid-winter to March.

tree.notes: Strong grower forming a broad pyramid with dense, drooping branches; bears on short spurs and also laterally on one- and two-year wood. Described as a regular bearer.

pollination.notes: Blossom is described as hardy and long-lasting. Brogdale records full bloom around 14 May, which corresponds to group 4.

climate.best_climates: Central European continental climates like Brandenburg, where it was bred for commercial growing.
climate.poor_climates: Inferred: hot summers, where Cox-type aromas fade; humid sites favour mildew.

health.other: Prone to powdery mildew but fairly scab-resistant; the fruit bruises easily in handling and transport.

grow_notes: Give it room, as it is vigorous and spreading, and an airy site to limit mildew. Pick carefully in October and store cool for eating after Christmas.

name: Upton Pyne
history: Raised by George Pyne of Denver Nurseries, Topsham, and introduced in 1910, named after the Devon village of Upton Pyne. Fruit was shown at the RHS in 1933.

look.description: Large, conical golden-yellow apple striped and mottled with pinkish orange.

taste.summary: Firm, rather coarse and juicy flesh with a fairly sharp flavour carrying a delicate pineapple note. Mainly a cooker, it cooks to a purée, but it can be eaten fresh later in the season.

tree.notes: Upright tree described as a regular bearer.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records full bloom around 11 May, which corresponds to group 3.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist south-west England, where it originated and is still grown locally.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; listed as suited to cool summers.

grow_notes: A good Devon dual-purpose apple for wetter western gardens. Store the fruit until after Christmas for fresh eating.
